# Customization and capability profiles

Pixel has two independent profile axes:

- `deploymentProfile` selects infrastructure: `prepared` uses existing private model
  and search endpoints; `reference` supplies reproducible local service definitions.
- `capabilityProfile` selects external limbs. Individual limb booleans in onboarding
  override the selected profile.

## Built-in capability profiles

| Profile | Email | Calendar | Social | Web | Operations | Frontier | Typical use |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `minimal` | off | off | off | off | off | off | private conversational core |
| `chief-of-staff` | on | on | off | on | off | off | inbox, schedule, and research |
| `research` | off | off | off | on | off | off | public-source research |
| `engineering-operator` | on | on | off | on | on | off | chief of staff plus fleet workflows |

Profiles live in `profiles/capabilities/` and contain no secrets. To customize a client,
select the nearest profile and override only the differences in its private onboarding
file:

```json
{
  "deploymentProfile": "prepared",
  "capabilityProfile": "engineering-operator",
  "socialLimbEnabled": true,
  "calendarLimbEnabled": false,
  "operationsPolicyFile": "/secure/acme/pixel-operations-policy.json",
  "frontierLimbEnabled": true,
  "frontierPolicyFile": "/secure/acme/pixel-frontier-policy.json",
  "frontierCredentialFile": "/secure/acme/openai-api-key"
}
```

For eligible Codex subscription access, start from
`deploy/frontier-broker/policy.chatgpt.example.json` and set
`frontierCredentialFile` to a private exported Codex `auth.json` instead. ChatGPT and
API-key usage have different billing and workspace-control boundaries; see
[FRONTIER-LIMB.md](FRONTIER-LIMB.md).

`./pixel limbs` shows the effective configuration. Reconfiguration removes disabled
tools from Pixel's allowlist and explicitly denies them; it also removes the related
plugin or service requirement. Disabling a limb does not delete private state. Review
retention separately before removing credentials, projections, artifacts, or logs.

## Customization-kit preview: signed projection limbs

Pixel 3.5 development includes a constrained pack workflow for offline local helpers.
The gateway adapter is generated by Pixel and can only read bounded JSON projections;
it has no network, credential, process, or write authority. The separate worker is
declared as offline and credential-free, can read only its signed pack and projection
state, and can write only its own projection directory. Every pack includes the same
signed hardened systemd service/timer boundary and baseline negative-case manifest.

Create and inspect an unsigned skeleton without granting it trust:

```bash
./pixel limb-kit generate host-health /absolute/work/host-health --name "Host health"
./pixel limb-kit validate /absolute/work/host-health
```

Customize `service/service.py` inside the declared boundary. Optional policy declarations
are generated with separate commands so their safe defaults and schema identities are
not hand-copied:

```bash
./pixel limb-kit add-local /absolute/work/host-health host-health-status
./pixel limb-kit add-operations /absolute/work/host-health host-health-actions \
  --target-placeholder private-host
./pixel limb-kit add-frontier /absolute/work/host-health host-health-review \
  --task-class plan_review
./pixel limb-kit validate /absolute/work/host-health
```

Local declarations are observe-only inventories tied to tools already declared by the
limb. Operations declarations can invoke only fixed `/usr/local/libexec/pixel-*` helpers,
remain inert without a private target mapping, and cannot grant production or change-tier
autonomy. Frontier declarations can only tighten an existing typed broker task: they may
reduce classifications or token bounds, disable it, or turn rehydration off. They cannot
add a prompt, task class, data category, provider, credential, or budget.

Do not put a token, password, private key, client data, raw source corpus, target hostname,
or provider configuration in the pack. Then sign the exact canonical tree with a dedicated
Ed25519 publisher key and verify it against a separately maintained allowed-signers file:

```bash
./pixel limb-kit sign /absolute/work/host-health \
  --signing-key /secure/pixel-limb-publisher --identity owner@example --confirm
./pixel limb-kit verify /absolute/work/host-health \
  --allowed-signers /secure/pixel-limb-allowed-signers --identity owner@example
```

Installation remains disabled and absent from onboarding. Activation is a separate,
confirmed operation. On Linux, `enable` verifies the installed receipt again, installs
the exact signed worker units under a new non-login per-pack identity, grants projection
read access only to the explicitly named gateway user, runs the worker once, enables its
timer, and only then updates private onboarding and the registry. Any failed step removes
the new service and restores onboarding. `--gateway-user "$USER"` is deliberately explicit;
do not substitute a shared or privileged account. Follow activation with Pixel's normal
configuration review:

```bash
sudo ./pixel limb-kit install /absolute/work/host-health \
  --allowed-signers /secure/pixel-limb-allowed-signers --identity owner@example --confirm
sudo ./pixel limb-kit enable host-health \
  --onboarding /secure/client/onboarding.json --gateway-user "$USER" --confirm
./pixel configure
./pixel plan
```

Use `status`, `disable`, `upgrade`, and `remove` for lifecycle work. Upgrades must be
newer, signed by the active publisher, explicitly declare migration from the active
version, and cannot lower the state schema. An enabled upgrade snapshots bounded
projection state and restores the old bytes, units, onboarding, and registry if the new
worker or commit fails. Disable verifies the installed units byte-for-byte before it
stops or removes them. Removal refuses an enabled pack or leftover worker units and
removes managed pack/projection state only after a registry transaction commits.

Enabling publishes signed Local capability receipts and restrictive Frontier receipts to
private onboarding. It does not activate an Operations action pack. Bind each action pack
to target IDs that already exist in the deployment-owned Operations policy, then re-run
the normal configure/plan/apply review:

```bash
sudo ./pixel limb-kit bind-operations host-health host-health-actions \
  --onboarding /secure/client/onboarding.json --target lab-runner --confirm
./pixel configure --answers /secure/client/onboarding.json --force
./pixel plan
```

Use `unbind-operations` to remove one mapping. Disable removes every Local/Frontier receipt
and any Operations mappings sourced from that limb. Upgrade preserves only mappings whose
policy-pack ID still exists, whose prior receipt exactly matches the active signed version,
and whose private targets still exist in the base policy; it then refreshes their signed
path, version, tree, and file hashes. Pixel configure verifies each no-follow file hash and
signed-limb provenance again; a Frontier declaration that would widen the deployment's
base policy fails closed.

This is still a development preview. Signed host-service confinement is generated,
validated, automatically provisioned, and rollback-tested on Linux; it is not yet a
stable third-party compatibility promise. Do not hand-edit or weaken an installed unit.
Networked workers and credential-bearing workers remain intentionally rejected. Policy
packs are data-only signed declarations; they do not run in the worker or gateway and do
not bypass the Source, Operations, or Frontier brokers.

## Adding a sensory limb

Follow the Source Broker pattern:

1. Put the source credential in a dedicated service identity, never the gateway.
2. Fetch raw content only in that service and reduce it to a small typed projection.
3. Remove instructions, secrets, active content, attachments, and unnecessary fields.
4. Mark every record untrusted and unable to authorize actions.
5. Give the OpenClaw plugin read-only access to the projection, scoped to Pixel's ID.
6. Add a separate actuator for writes; do not let the read plugin reuse its credential.
7. Add injection, stale-data, malformed-input, and disabled-limb tests.

## Adding an operational capability

Follow the Operations Broker pattern. Add a root-owned, narrowly implemented helper if
the operation cannot be expressed safely as a fixed argv. Then add a named policy
action with:

- the smallest target set and allowed root;
- an accurate risk tier and short timeout;
- anchored parameter patterns with tight length limits;
- dedicated or ephemeral isolation for automatic staging work;
- exclusive-target serialization for state changes;
- bounded, secret-free output and a deterministic success condition.

Add failure, timeout, cancellation, hostile-output, and replay tests before enabling it
for a client. A new backend must preserve the same external broker authority, pinned
target identity, immutable planning, cancellation, output bounding, and approval
semantics.

For reusable capabilities, add actions to a sanitized action-pack file with a
placeholder target; map that placeholder only in private onboarding. Declare the
target environment honestly. Keep standing grants to lab/test/staging work. Production
or `change` automation should be an exact, short-lived operator lease with parameter,
execution, concurrency, runtime, output, artifact, and failure budgets. A managed
action must verify its result and automatically restore a known prior state on failure.
See [OPERATIONS-AUTONOMY.md](OPERATIONS-AUTONOMY.md).

## Adding a Frontier task class

Do not add a generic prompt. Define an exact request schema with the minimum structural
fields, explicit classification/category rules, deterministic byte/token bounds, and a
strict output schema. Extend the broker compiler, plan hash, workspace contract,
provider fake, disabled-limb rendering, secret/identifier corpus, malformed-input,
replay/concurrency, and clean-room tests together. New raw source, file, repository,
message, URL, credential, or regulated-record paths are out of scope; use a local
projection or deterministic feature extraction instead. See
[FRONTIER-LIMB.md](FRONTIER-LIMB.md).

## Replication boundary

Git contains code, examples, schemas, tests, and sanitized templates. Each deployment
must generate its own OAuth client, token, model and Frontier credentials, Operations SSH key, host-key
pins, private policy, workspace memory, and backups. Package a client handoff with
`./pixel package`; never copy another deployment's `.env`, `.generated`, `.runtime`,
OpenClaw state, broker state, or live workspace into the repository.
